entries.title: Germany news: Spy chief warns Russia conflict risk growing
entries.summary: Moscow is already waging a "shadow war" against Europe, the head of Germany's foreign intelligence service says. The Left Party is taking a case over remarks by the CDU's Katherina Reiche to a top court. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Spy chief warns Russia conflict risk growing

Published October 5, 2026last updated October 5, 2026

Moscow is already waging a "shadow war" against Europe, the head of Germany's foreign intelligence service says. The Left Party is taking a case over remarks by the CDU's Katherina Reiche to a top court. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The BND foreign intelligence agency has noted a "new, more dangerous dimension" to the confrontation with Russia.
  • The Left Party is suing Economy Minister Katherina Reiche at the Constitutional Court for using official government channels to criticize it
  • Grassroots groups from junior coalition partners the SPD have objected to several elements in a proposed reform of labor laws
  • A draft bill envisages making it easier for victims of domestic violence to move away from perpetrators
  • 100,000 households have received an e-vehicle subsidy since May, the environment minister says

Here is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany hitting the headlines on Monday, October 5, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Chinese high-tech could be security risk — domestic intelligence agency

Chinese high-tech could be security risk — domestic intelligence agency

High-tech goods from China, such as electric vehicles or even robot vacuum cleaners, could represent a security risk, the BfV domestic intelligence agency has warned.

BfV head Sinan Selen told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin that the issue was of "great concern" to him.

"I already see substantial shortcomings that create potential for abuse," he said.

Data collected via the products could be passed on to "state agencies", he said, leading to risks including "potential shutdown of entire products."

"In terms of resilience and availability (this) could confront us with problems," he said.

The warning comes as sales of high-tech products to Germany are growing and Chinese manufacturers compete ever more strongly with their German counterparts.

Skip next section Deutsche Telekom targets billions in AI savings

Deutsche Telekom targets billions in AI savings

Deutsche Telekom plans to use artificial intelligence and automation to cut annual costs by around €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) by 2030.

The target covers the German telecommunications giant's operations outside the United States.

Deutsche Telekom is already using AI for repetitive tasks in network operations, customer service, software development and administration.

Its "Frag Magenta" chatbot handled around 2.6 million customer service calls in the first half of 2026, the company said.

At T-Mobile US, in which Deutsche Telekom holds a majority stake, AI agents now handle 40% of customer contacts.

Outside the US, Deutsche Telekom expects savings from AI and automation to reach €1.1 billion by 2027 and €2.5 billion by 2030.

"AI is fundamentally changing Deutsche Telekom," CEO Tim Höttges said. He said the technology was improving networks and customer service while opening up new business models."

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany trainer Klopp's first internationals

IN DEPTH: Germany trainer Klopp's first internationals

The German football team has had its first four international matches under its new coach, Jürgen Klopp — a mixture of success, failure and in-betweens.

DW analyzes Klopp's methods and relationship with the team as shown over the past couple of months in this article: Klopp's first Germany internationals: What did we learn?

Skip next section Social Democrat groups oppose coalition's working week reform

Social Democrat groups oppose coalition's working week reform

Grassroots groups within the Social Democrats (SPD) — the junior partner in Germany's conservative-led coalition government — have spoken out against plans to "flexibilize" the working week in a position paper.

In question is a paragraph in the coalition agreement that speaks of "the possibility of a weekly rather than a daily maximum working time."

The conservative Christian Democrat (CDU)-Christian Social Union (CSU) bloc has pushed to have a maximum number of hours that can be worked per week rather than the current daily standard limit of eight hours.

Although the four SPD groups fundamentally accept the idea, they are calling for strict controls, among other things wanting collective labor agreements under which both parties work out details as "a necessary prerequisite."

They also say exceptions should made in certain sectors where illegal employment is prevalent.

Employers' associations in June objected to the idea of collective labor agreements as a coercive measure when it was put forward by the Labor Ministry, leading to its retraction, with the CDU saying that it went against the coalition agreement.

The position paper submitted by the SPD groups could thus lead to a new split in the coalition, stating as it does: "It is not in keeping with a modern reform of working hours regulation or a better compatibility of work and family when bosses can decide alone when employees can knock off work."

Skip next section German court sets limits on deportation detention

German court sets limits on deportation detention

Germany's Federal Court of Justice (BGH) has ruled that a person facing deportation cannot be detained as a flight risk simply because their past behavior suggests they might try to avoid being deported.

The case concerned a stateless Palestinian man who sought asylum at a police station in Germany in April 2023. Austrian authorities had already issued a decision requiring him to return.

A court in the German city of Duisburg ordered the man detained while his transfer was being arranged.

The courts argued that his previous actions indicated a risk that he would try to evade deportation. He had lived in Austria since 2020, where two asylum applications had been rejected, and had also applied for asylum in Belgium and Germany.

But the man had never explicitly said that he intended to avoid deportation.

The BGH ruled that his behavior alone was not enough to establish this particular ground for detention.

A person's words do not necessarily have to state the intention literally, the judges said. But it must be "clear and unambiguous" from what the person says and the circumstances that they intend to evade deportation.

The court found that the man's detention from May 7 to June 6, 2023 had therefore violated his rights.

German immigration law provides several other grounds on which people can be detained pending deportation.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Two German scientists in Nobel-winning trio

IN DEPTH: Two German scientists in Nobel-winning trio

Peter Hegemann from Germany's Humbolt University and Georg Nagel from the University of Würzburg have won this year's Nobel Prize in medicine alongside their US colleague, Karl Deisseroth.

You can read more about their achievements in this article: German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine

Skip next section Germany at risk of 'violent conflict' with Russia — intelligence chief

Germany at risk of 'violent conflict' with Russia — intelligence chief

Germany is facing a growing risk of a violent confrontation with Russia as Moscow continues a campaign of hybrid warfare with other countries in Europe, the head ‌of ⁠Germany's BND ⁠foreign intelligence service warned on Monday.

Speaking before the Bundestag at ​the ‌annual public hearing of intelligence chiefs, Martin Jäger said: "The confrontation we are facing with Russia has ​taken on a new, more dangerous dimension."

"Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled ‌in a violent conflict with Russia — the ‌attempted ​attack in Leipzig is just one example," he said.

"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," he added.

Jäger was referring to a drone attack at Leipzig airport in August that the German government has blamed on Russia.

Russia has repeatedly denied any intention of attacking ​NATO

countries, with President Vladimir Putin, however, saying on Thursday: "But if we are subjected to aggression, we will have no choice but to respond."

Skip next section Draft bill aims to help domestic abuse victims move house

Draft bill aims to help domestic abuse victims move house

The Justice Ministry has put forward a draft bill making it easier for domestic abuse victims to leave joint tenancy contracts and obliging perpetrators to pay for any ensuing costs.

"The path to a self-determined and safe life after domestic abuse is often still a long one," Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig told newspapers from the Funke media group.

"We want to make it a bit easier," she added.

She said the draft bill aimed to give domestic abuse victims clear legal rights against their abusers, including being able to demand that the latter pay any costs arising from the premature termination of the joint lease.

More protection for others in the household

The bill also envisages increased protection for children and relatives of victims.

Under current German law, family courts can impose bans on domestic abusers taking up contact with or approaching their victims but not other members of the same household.

Hubig said the draft law foresaw such protections being extended to other people dependent on the abuser without any separate application being made.

According to police statistics, nearly 266,000 people in Germany were affected by domestic abuse in 2024, 70% of them women and girls.

The Justice Ministry has said the real figure is likely to be much higher, estimating that 95% of cases go unreported.

Skip next section E-vehicle subsidy program has 'exceeded our expectations' — environment minister

E-vehicle subsidy program has 'exceeded our expectations' — environment minister

Since May, the German government has paid out subsidies to 100,000 households wanting to procure an electric vehicle, Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the mass-circulation Bild newspaper on Monday.

Schneider, from junior coalition partner the Social Democrats (SPD), said the program, worth €3 billion ($3.36 billion), had "far exceeded our expectations."

He said that every additional electric vehicle protected households from high fuel prices and made the county less dependent on expensive oil imports and international conflicts.

According to the Bild article, half of households applying for the subsidy had a maximum annual income of €45,000 and three-quarters of them €60,000.

Schneider said he found it particularly important that this graduation of payments according to income functioned properly.

Preliminary assessments have shown that less than 15% of households that applied for the subsidy were looking to buy vehicles from China, contradicting expert views that Chinese automakers would profit the most.

Skip next section Left Party takes Economy Minister Reiche to top court

Left Party takes Economy Minister Reiche to top court

The Left Party is taking a row about a remark made by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche to the Constitutional Court after Reiche failed to give a declaration to cease and desist on time.

Reiche had posted a remark on the official Instagram site of her ministry saying: "Antisemitism and expropriation endanger Germany and the economy."

The comment refers first to the unproven accusation that the Left Party is antisemitic in its ideology and then to the Left Party's plan to socialize apartments from corporate landlords in a bid to reduce skyrocketing rents in the capital.

Reiche doubled down on her criticism of the socialist party in comments she made during a visit to Ukraine over the weekend, telling the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild she feared a national loss of growth if a leftist coalition took power in Berlin.

"What the Left Party represents here in Berlin and the people that it represents is dangerous not only for Berlin but for our country," she said.

The Berlin branch of the Left Party has accused the Christian Democrats (CDU), to which Reiche and Chancellor Friedrich Merz belong, of carrying out a "large-scale campaign" against its top candidate, Elif Eralp, who won recent state elections in Berlin.

It has taken legal action over similar statements on CDU interior ministry websites in various states, criticizing the use of official government channels to denigrate another party.

The ministries in Saxony and Schleswig Holstein withdrew the statements, but those in Baden-Württemberg, Brandenburg and Hesse have so far not done so.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

DW's newsroom in Bonn bids guten Tag to all its users!

The Left Party's victory in state elections in Berlin continues to make waves, with conservatives around the country not amused at the prospect of a socialist-led government in the capital region.

The party is fighting back against what it sees as an illegal campaign against it by the Christian Democrats (CDU) and is now taking the economy minister to a top court over remarks she made on her ministry's website.

The environment minister, Carsten Schneider from the Social Democrats (SPD), has voiced satisfaction over the number of households taking advantage of government subsidies to procure an electric vehicle.

And the justice minister wants to help victims of domestic violence escape the proximity with their tormentors by making it easier for them to move house.

For more on these and other stories, please read on!

entries.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
entries.summary: A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia has died, and nearly 200 of her contacts are under medical observation. Russian authorities deny a link to the bacterial infection. The US is monitoring the situation.
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia has died, and nearly 200 of her contacts are under medical observation. Russian authorities deny a link to the bacterial infection. The US is monitoring the situation.

What you need to know about plague

  • There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
  • The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
  • Bubonic plague is the most common form, it does not spread from person to person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure.
  • If the the bacteria reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is highly contagious as it can pass from person to person through the air, via coughing, for example.
  • If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.

Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.

She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, two hospitals and a children's clinic were placed under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."

Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection

All that is known for certain, at time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.

The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.

Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.

A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.

What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?

Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

All are caused by the same bacterium.

What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.

Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours

Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.

Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). 

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.

Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.

The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: Klopp's first Germany internationals: What did we learn?
entries.summary: Jürgen Klopp has done things a little differently since becoming Germany coach. Casting a wider net for talent and trying to connect with players and country haven't make an immediate impact, but he is not bowed.
entries.content:
Germany

Klopp's first Germany internationals: What did we learn?

October 5, 2026

Jürgen Klopp has done things a little differently since becoming Germany coach. Casting a wider net for talent and trying to connect with players and country haven't made an immediate impact, but he is not bowed.

Four games, three goals, two draws, one loss and one win. Jürgen Klopp would have hoped for better results from his first international break as Germany coach. But though the comfortable win over Serbia (2-0), draws against the Netherlands (1-1) and Greece (0-0) and a shock loss to Greece (0-1) in Germany leave them third out of four in their Nations League group, Klopp saw mostly positives.

"Everyone showed what they're made of; everyone earned their place. We've shown signs that we can do some things better than people gave us credit for. I wanted to get something going, and I definitely saw that happen," he said after Sunday's 0-0 draw in Thessaloniki.

For all the positivity of the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach, the four matches have, in reality, been a mixed bag for Germany.

It's a long road back to the top

Having fallen in the last 32 of the 2026 World Cup and exited in the group stage in 2022, Germany's footballing stock has never been lower.

Klopp tried to address this by casting his net wider, announcing a 44-man squad that split over the matches. He then said this would be a one off, but that his strategy of trying to find a diamond in the relative rough who could adapt to the international game had given him valuable insights.

"Hard work, lots of information — these guys are brimming with talent," he said of those given a surprise opportunity.

"People were saying that German soccer was at rock bottom and that there was no talent. ... They're not lacking in talent."

While Klopp may have seen potential, and has credit in the bank from his past work, he will need to turn that into results before too long.

Klopp leans on emotion and unity

While much has been said about Klopp's success in imprinting his trademark Gegenpressing (counter press) style early on, he is also a coach who places a high value on connection. Throughout the international break, he has worn a cap emblazoned with the slogan "Einer von 83 millionen” (One of 83 million) in a reference to the German population and an attempt to unify in a country divided by the rise of the far-right AfD party.

He addressed the issue in his opening press conference and then reiterated his position after some social media users branded the team "not white enough" after their loss to Greece.

"There is no reason to give these people any thought. They aren't getting any of my attention. I have little time for stupidity in real life and none on social media either," Klopp said in answer to a question posed by DW.

As well as speaking honestly about his country, Klopp has been open with his new players.

"He has a very good rapport with every player. He tries to reach out to every player and make them feel good, that they're important and that they deserve to be here," said Florian Wirtz, who went on to label his coach as a "master" at managing relationships.

With limited time together, forming bonds between player, coach and country can elevate a national team. It may prove to be more important than any tactical plans.

Havertz injury highlights lack of striking depth

One of the key men in the more senior squad that started the opener against the Netherlands, Kai Havertz limped off after 29 minutes. He was replaced by Eintracht Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib while Nick Woltemade (on loan at Juventus from Newcastle) and Jonathan Burkhardt, also Frankfurt, were also tested up front over the four games.

None of the replacements scored, with Woltemade guilty of a particularly bad miss against Serbia and Burkhardt having a goal disallowed against Greece on Sunday. While all have potential and have enjoyed strong patches of form in their careers, none is tried and tested at the top level, and none is playing in the Champions League. With Havertz being somewhat injury prone, Klopp needs someone to emerge as a viable backup.

Musiala and Wirtz key but both have question marks

Injury is also, sadly, beginning to be a major feature of Jamal Musiala's career. He picked up a thigh injury in the warmup to the Netherlands game that may keep him out for a month. He's also missed games this season due to a neurological condition and missed the first half of last season with a broken leg which came soon after another lengthy spell out. At his best, he is probably Germany's brightest attacking spark, but it's been a while since that level has been seen.

For Wirtz, the issue is slightly different. He was excellent in the win over a limited Serbia team, scoring one and creating the other. It was a reminder of a talent that has been largely dormant at Liverpool where he's shown his creative best only in glimpses. He followed it up with a decent display against Greece but saw Burkahrdt inadvertently block his goalbound header. There were signs Klopp's system may suit him.

"He's really gotten us on board with his philosophy," said Wirtz of his coach. "I enjoy it myself, too. I get to show my strengths when we have possession."

Klopp will need more of the same from Wirtz, who captained the side in Greece, if Germany are to move forward.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Bosnia election: New technology might have stopped votes being cast on behalf of dead voters, but the result remains unchanged
entries.summary: New technology has stopped votes being cast on behalf of dead or absent voters, and turnout has fallen to a record low. But it was a case of deja vu in Bosnia's elections with the same parties winning.
entries.content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina

Bosnia: Tougher on fraud, nationalist parties still win

October 5, 2026

New technology has stopped votes being cast on behalf of dead or absent voters, and turnout has fallen to a record low. But it was a case of deja vu in Bosnia's elections with the same parties winning.

Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the polls on October 4 with new technology that was meant to end years of vote-rigging.

Chief among the abuses was the casting of ballots in the name of deceased voters who had lingered for years on outdated voter rolls.

At just over 40%, turnout was the lowest since the Bosnian War ended in 1995, in part because the old tricks no longer worked.

In earlier elections, allegations kept surfacing that votes were being cast in the name of people who had died or long since moved abroad. Others said voters cast their ballot multiple times or that blank ballots were added after polls closed to make the turnout look higher.

The voter registry, packed with names of people who had passed away or left the country, was the perfect tool for all of this.

New technology, same old politics

This time, however, every polling station used biometric fingerprint checks.

This represented a clear step forward in making voter identification far harder to manipulate.

Still, the biggest story of this election is not technical. Three nationalist parties won, each within its own community: the SNSD among Serbs, the SDA among Bosniaks and the HDZ BiH among Croats.

The dead may have been struck from the voter rolls, but political trends have not shifted.

For readers who know Bosnia only vaguely, a little background helps: The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, but it also split the country into two entities: Republika Srpska, which has a Serb majority, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a Bosniak-Croat majority.

A three-member presidency runs the state, and each of the three peoples elects its own member.

That is why elections here are rarely about wages and prices and are instead almost always about who is perceived to be a threat.

Republika Srpska and the return of a fallen leader

For Milorad Dodik, the most powerful Serb politician in Bosnia, this election was a political resurrection.

In 2025, Dodik was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the high representative, the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

He was sanctioned by the US in 2022, although those sanctions were lifted late last year. Even so, his party, the SNSD, virtually swept the board in Republika Srpska.

Savo Minic became president of Republika Srpska, and Zeljka Cvijanovic kept the Serb seat in the presidency. Both are members of the SNSD.

The party also did very well in the entity's parliament. Neither the sanctions nor Dodik's conviction and the loss of his mandate hurt the party. Voters were not choosing an individual. They were choosing their "side."

Dodik lost no time in declaring what comes next.

He announced a return to what he refers to as the "original Dayton." In practice, that means undoing the powers the state has gained since 1995 — from the judiciary to the army. To an outside observer, that sounds like a technical phrase. In reality, it is a program for dismantling the state step by step.

"That means we are returning the army to Republika Srpska, the border police, the intelligence service and everything that the high representatives once took away," said Dodik.

A deal between Serbs and Croats?

The opposition offered no serious resistance. It was divided and had no convincing message.

Voters who did not want Dodik had nowhere to turn, so most stayed home. Low turnout favored the side with the most disciplined party machine.

That raises a question that will shape what happens in Bosnia in the coming year. Dodik's conviction kept him out of the direct race in these elections. But for months, there has been talk of a way out.

If representatives of the SNSD and the HDZ BiH enter the presidency, they could pardon him — whatever the third member decides. Bosnian media have reported that this was a pre-election deal between Dodik and the HDZ BiH leader, Dragan Covic. Dodik could then return as prime minister of Republika Srpska, a post he has held before.

Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Troika defeated

The picture in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is different, but the outcome is the same.

The parties of the so-called "Troika," a multi-ethnic liberal political alliance, suffered a defeat. They came to power at this level after the international high representative, a foreigner with the authority to impose laws, changed the election law.

Voters saw no benefit from that experiment. The SDA, the largest Bosniak nationalist party, won the most seats and did well.

The paradox is that SDA president Bakir Izetbegovic lost the race for the presidency. He is the son of Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's first president and one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement. The winner was Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats (SDP), who kept the Bosniak seat.

So, the party won the election, but its leader lost. The son of the man who signed Dayton is now shut out of the institution Dayton created.

"The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia. Let the will of the people be the law of the land," Becirovic said as he declared victory.

A Croat surprise

The same pattern holds among Croats. Darijana Filipovic of the HDZ BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party. Filipovic spent years as an aide to Covic, the Bosnian Croat leader.

"HDZ BiH has shown it is brave enough to take a road others would not dare. Who would have dared to nominate me? To some too young, but a surprise to everyone," Filipovic said after the vote.

Three peoples, three nationalist parties, three victories, and not one conversation about how to keep people in the country.

What this means for the state

The most important thing about these elections is not the numbers but the makeup of the presidency. Two women will sit in it: Cvijanovic of the SNSD and Filipovic of the HDZ BiH. Anyone who tries to sell that as a breakthrough for women in politics has missed the point.

Both come from parties that, in different ways, do not want the state in its current form. Both could also decide the fate of a man convicted of defying the international oversight of Dayton.

The HDZ BiH has long demanded a third, Croat entity. The SNSD wants autonomy for Republika Srpska. One side wants to split the state into three, the other into two, but they share the aim of making it smaller.

So, the presidency, which should symbolize a shared state, is again made up of people who feel like guests in it.

All of this is happening as the Western Balkans again becomes a stage for rivalry between Russia, the EU and the US. Dodik openly thanked both Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after his party's victory.

Bosnia has entered a new electoral era with new technology and old politics. Young people are leaving the country in droves. The dead no longer vote, but the living have stopped believing that anything can be different.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine for research on brain activity
entries.summary: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the award for discoveries that provide new insights into how we might treat blindness, depression, addiction and dementia.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine

October 5, 2026

Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the award for discoveries that provide new insights into how we might treat blindness, depression, addiction and dementia.

The Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has gone to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, the academy announced on Monday.

The trio won the award for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, which combines the methods of optics and genetics to create a form of non-invasive stimulation of neurons.

The Nobel Assembly said that optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain, as researchers have been "able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders."

"The impact of optogenetics extends far beyond understanding the healthy brain, it has also helped revealed how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression, addiction and dementia," Abdel El Manira, Nobel committee member and professor of neuroscience, said after the announcement was made.

In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. Researchers hope that the field could lead to treatments for neurological and sensory disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.

Who are the winners?

Hegemann is considered to be the leading expert in photobiology and one of the founding fathers of optogenetics. He is a professor of neuroscience at the Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany.

Georg Nagel is a biophysicist and professor at of neurophysiology at the University of Würzburg, Germany. Karl Deisseroth is a professor of bioengineering and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University in the US.

The trio came togther as Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae could swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.

Deisseroth then joined in to work with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.

Medicine is the first of Nobels announced this week

The award for medicine is the first Nobel prize to be awarded this week, with laureates set to be named in physics, chemistry, literature and peace in the days up to Friday.

Last year's prize was awarded jointly to Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell of the United States and Shimun Sakaguchi of Japan for "for their discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance."

The prizes will be presented at ceremonies in Stockholm, Sweden on December 10.

Each prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor, which is equivalent to just over €1 million or $1.2 million.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: As rising seas threaten low-lying Pacific Islands, regional leaders call on the world to take climate more seriously
entries.summary: For Pacific island nations, climate change is no distant threat. As seas rise, they're bringing the real-time consequences of a warming planet directly to world leaders in Tuvalu.
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

For Pacific island nations, climate change is no distant threat. As seas rise, they're bringing the real-time consequences of a warming planet directly to world leaders in Tuvalu.

For Pacific islanders, the ocean is a source of food, livelihoods and cultural identity. But a changing climate is turning that lifeline into a threat, as rising global temperatures drive sea levels higher.

"When there's a low tide, you'll actually see foundations of homes, you see burial grounds of your ancestors...," said Anne Rasmussen, lead climate negotiator for the Association of Small Island States (AOSIS), adding that higher seas are making some land uninhabitable.

This week, a handful of world leaders are in Fiji with ministers and climate negotiators from around 60 countries to discuss the outstanding issues surrounding the UN-led international climate conference that kicks off in Turkey next month.

Pacific leaders see these talks ahead of COP31 as an opportunity to highlight the increasing urgency facing their low-lying islands.

"It's actually to bring the people who are continuing to turn a blind eye and deaf ears to the communities of the vulnerable islands to these effects," Rasmussen told DW, emphasizing the importance of holding these talks in the Pacific.

"It showcases the vulnerability. It showcases the impacts that are already happening. And it also brings the community, the real people at the front line, to participate in these pre-COPs," she added.

On the frontlines of climate change

Leaders attending the event will first travel to the island of Tuvalu, which scientists predict could be one of the first countries to become inhabitable due to rising sea levels caused by human-driven climate change.

At the UN General Assembly last month, Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told delegates that sea level rise is a "present reality."

"Tuvalu's message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come."

At an average of just two meters above sea level, the archipelago has faced more frequent and severe flooding as water levels have risen.

"Having back-to-back hurricanes and storms, having back-to-back significant floods...it really sets back countries and affects communities," Rasmussen, who comes from the Pacific island of Samoa, told DW. "People are losing their homes."

She also said rising sea levels are contaminating freshwater sources with salt, which threatens crops. In addition, hotter oceans mean corals lose the algae they rely on to survive, causing them to bleach and become less able to accommodate the diverse marine life that local populations rely on for their income.

Overshooting agreed limits on temperature rise

Although only few leaders from outside the region are expected at the conference, negotiators from countries including Germany, Mexico and South Korea will be present. Efforts to limit planetary heating are expected to be high on the agenda.

Pacific leaders are pushing for a renewed commitment to keep global temperature rise capped to 1.5 degrees (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) — a limit that was agreed on by world leaders at the Paris climate conference in 2015.

A UN report released in September said under a best-case scenario, temperatures were likely to reach at least 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels. The study added that it is still possible to "bring temperatures down."

Natasha Green, Australia country lead for climate think-tank E3G , said small island and least developing states are calling for countries to work together to enable vulnerable nations to "adapt and build resilience to the worsening impacts of climate change."

Tricky questions of climate finance

A key issue at this week's talks will be climate finance. Poorer nations, which have done little to contribute to rising global temperatures, yet are feeling some of the worst impacts, have long called on richer, higher-emitting countries to provide more money to help them adapt to a hotter world.

Laura Schäfer, international climate policy head of division at environment and human rights nonprofit, Germanwatch, said she would like to see Australia, who holds the COP presidency, "address tricky questions." 



Such as "how to include carbon majors, including the big fossil [fuel] industry in paying for climate damages like the ones we have just seen in Nepal." 

Also on the agenda will be a the non-use of fossil fuels for creating energy. At the 2023 climate conference, countries agreed for the first time to move towards a future that doesn’t rely on oil, gas and coal. Since then, however, there has been little progress.

Earlier this year just under 60 states took part in the first International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

Scientists say an end to burning these polluting sources of energy is the only way to bring global temperature levels back under agreed limits. And thereby prevent some of the worst impacts of climate change — like the rising sea levels affecting island states and coastline communities.

"It's really important that the COPs continue to progress and elevate the commitment [...] to transition away from fossil fuels," said Green.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Israel's mental health crisis in the wake of Oct. 7 attacks
entries.summary: More than a third of Israelis have shown symptoms of mental health conditions, a report found. Three years after the October 7 attack, the country's health system is still struggling to come to terms with its effects.
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

More than a third of Israelis have shown symptoms of mental health conditions, a report found. Three years after the October 7 attack, the country's health system is still struggling to come to terms with its effects.

Warning: This article contains references to death by suicide that some readers may find disturbing.

As October 7's third anniversary approaches, Ronen Shalev's body tells him something's coming.

"You start shivering," he tells DW. "It's not just one day and you move on. We have many graves to visit, many families to meet. It's a difficult time and you feel it in your body."

Both of his children attended the Nova Party in Israel's south, where almost 400 people were killed in a terrorist attack carried out by Palestinian militant group Hamas and its affiliates in Gaza. In total, roughly 1,200 people were killed in the attack and around 250 were taken hostage.

The attack triggered the war in Gaza, during which Israel has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced much of the territory's population.

Shalev's son, Roee, was shot and hospitalized, but he survived. Roee's partner, Mapal Adam, was killed in front of his eyes. Shalev's daughter, Lior, also made it out.

Shortly after that day, Shalev's wife Gavriela went missing, before her body was found in a burned car with a goodbye letter. "She couldn't handle the sorrow from that day," Shalev says.

At the same time, his son Roee's post-traumatic symptoms started emerging, mostly in the form of extreme mood swings. "He went to treatment to please me, but he didn't really believe in it. He thought he was OK, that he was strong," Shalev remembers.

Two years after Gavriela's death, Roee couldn't take it anymore, either.

"I'm alive, but I'm dead within," Roee wrote in his goodbye message, which he posted on his Instagram account. "I'm sorry."

A country in post-traumatic state

Since October 2023, Israel has been grappling with a mental health crisis of unprecedented scale.

According to a report by Israel's State Comptroller from February 2025, some 39% of the Israeli public reported suffering from post-traumatic symptoms, depression, anxiety or a combination of the three, on a medium or severe level.

This amounts to some 3 million people, 600,000 of whom could suffer severely. However, the report also found that the number of people receiving mental health treatment had only risen by 1% since October 7, 2023, a difference of around 60,000 people.

Among the affected groups are survivors of the attack, as well as people evacuated from their homes in Israel's south and north due to the war.

Noga Dagan-Buzaglo is a researcher with the Adva Center, a think tank focusing on inequality in Israeli society. She wrote an extensive paper about Israel's mental health system and its challenges post-October 7.

She tells DW that while the country's mental health budget did increase due to the war, it was too little, too late, as the health system faced an ongoing crisis that was not handled properly.

"The biggest challenge is convincing people to work in Israel's public mental health system, both due to lower wages in comparison to the private sector and due to an overload of work," she says.

Sedatives often the go-to solution

The current situation affects mental health professionals, too. Research by the University of Haifa found that 84% of the therapists who treated people affected by the October 7 attack showed traumatic symptoms themselves, and some 45% of them said they feel mentally exhausted.

Israel's Health Ministry has repeatedly said it has increased funding and job openings for the country's public mental health system, but staffing shortages remain, especially in peripheral regions in the far north and south.

Because of these issues, the report said waiting times for treatment through Israel's public healthcare system were longer than six months. In some cases, Dagan-Buzaglo says, patients had to wait more than a year before receiving help.

Mental health NGOs and volunteers try to fill the gaps, often struggling themselves under the workload. This also leads to an increased use of prescription medications. Some people turn to substances like alcohol and drugs.

The Israeli Ministry of Health said earlier this year that it had registered a rise of between 13% and 17% in the prescription of sedatives, sleep aids and antidepressants.

Those who suffer from the situation the most are the ones who cannot afford to pay a private therapist. Dagan-Buzaglo labels the Israeli public health system's response to the situation as "simply bad."

Soldiers at risk

Combat soldiers have received a special focus when it comes to Israel's mental health crisis.

Statistics published by the Israeli parliament and the IDF suggest a sharp rise of suicide cases among reservists: from a maximum of one annual case in the six years preceding the war to 11 cases in 2024, as well as nine cases investigated as suspected suicides in 2025. This does not include ex-soldiers who committed suicide due to trauma after the end of their service.

Dagan-Buzaglo, a researcher at the Adva Center, says that while professionals receive better pay and conditions working for the army, the lack of personnel is still apparent. "In the army, too, the length and quality of treatment are by far not at an adequate level."

To start solving the problem for both civilians and soldiers, she believes the system needs more support. "We have to acknowledge the fact that trauma is not over after a year. This means investing money."

Breaking the taboo

Ronen Shalev holds regular lectures and talks about the importance of mental health, often to groups of soldiers. He believes this is the best way to continue his son's legacy of fighting to live on.

Shalev, who himself was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), says he made a choice to live his life to its fullest.

His message: The taboo regarding suicidality — which still exists across Israeli society — needs to be broken. "This is especially true regarding those who say they are strong. They're the scary ones as they're less likely to receive treatment."

For Shalev, speaking publicly about his family's experience has become part of his own recovery — and a way to encourage others to seek help before they reach a crisis point.

"Life, with all its pain, is still worth deciding in favor of," he said.

If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://befrienders.org/

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Israel observes October 7 anniversary with national memorial day
entries.summary: Israel is holding memorial ceremonies nationwide for those killed in the October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attacks and soldiers who died in the ensuing war.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel marks October 7 anniversary as national memorial day

October 5, 2026

Israel is holding memorial ceremonies nationwide for those killed in the October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attacks and soldiers who died in the ensuing war.

Israel is observing a national memorial day on Monday for those killed in the October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attacks and the soldiers who died in the Gaza war, Israeli media reported.

Two state ceremonies are being held at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, where President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other senior officials are expected to attend, The Jerusalem Post reported.

More memorial events, rallies and ceremonies are planned across the country with schools, municipalities and communities also holding events throughout the day.

Flags at state institutions, police stations, prisons and military bases were lowered to half-mast, reports said. The memorial fell on October 5 this year due to the Hebrew calendar, which is lunisolar.

October 7 terror attacks set of chain of events

The Hamas terror attack on October 7 killed some 1,200 people in Israel, with the Palestinian militant also taking another 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.

The October 7, 2023, attacks had massive consequences not only for Israeli society but also for Palestinians in Gaza, where Hamas had maintained power since the territory last held elections in 2006.

Following the Hamas attacks, the Israeli military began a war targeting Hamas in Gaza. The European Union, as well as the United States, Germany, and other countries, classify Hamas as a terrorist organization.

Israel's war on Hamas left more than 73,650 Palestinians dead in Gaza , most of them civilians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calls snap election
entries.summary: The Spanish prime minister had repeatedly insisted he would serve out his four-year term, with elections scheduled for 2027. The move comes after a major defeat for his coalition's proposed housing reforms.
entries.content:
Spain

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calls snap election

October 5, 2026

The Spanish prime minister had repeatedly insisted he would serve out his four-year term, with elections scheduled for 2027. The move comes after a major defeat for his coalition's proposed housing reforms.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an early general election on Monday, bringing forward a vote that had been scheduled for 2027.

Sanchez announced the decision in a statement at Madrid's Moncloa Palace after a weekend of consultations with his closest advisers.

What did Sanchez say?

"It is time for Spaniards to decide what future you want," Sanchez said.

The announcement of the November 29 vote follows a parliamentary defeat for his minority government on Friday, when lawmakers rejected measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis.

Sanchez framed the election as a choice over Spain's future direction, saying voters must decide whether the country joins what he called a "far-right wave" or continues on a path of "openness, social justice and environmental responsibility."

He said he trusted Spanish voters to make that choice.

"To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez said, adding that his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament."

The decision comes despite Sanchez repeatedly insisting in recent months that his government would complete its four-year term.

What led up to the snap election?

The election follows mounting public pressure over housing costs, with large protests across the country.

Tens of thousands of people marched in Madrid and other Spanish cities on Saturday to demand more affordable housing.

Opposition parties on Friday rejected government measures that included automatically extending tenancy contracts and restricting the eviction of vulnerable tenants.

The parliamentary defeat highlighted the difficulties Sanchez's minority coalition has faced in passing legislation. Spain has also been operating for several years under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan approved under Sanchez.

Housing protests intensified after the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for decades. Hundreds of protesters have since set up a tent camp in central Madrid.

Recent opinion polls have generally put the opposition conservative Popular Party ahead of Sanchez's Socialist Workers' Party.

entries.title: Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
entries.summary: Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.
entries.content:
Yemen

Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis

October 5, 2026

Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.

Yemen's Saudi-backed government on Sunday announced a new military operation to retake territory held by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, as fighting intensified around the key southwestern city of Taiz.

"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.

The announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.

More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.

How did the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthis escalate?

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.

A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.

As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.

The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.
